rules.message: `updateMany`/`deleteMany` called with no `where:` clause anywhere in the enclosing function — a whole-table write, not a filtered subset. IF NO FILTER ALREADY SCOPES THIS CALL: add a `where:` filter that scopes the write, or mark a genuinely full-table write explicitly. What it actually reads is a LEXICAL token search for `where:` over the enclosing function body, with no structural link between that token and this call, and it leaks in BOTH directions (measured 2026-08-18). It over-reports when the filter is real but spells no `where:` token in this function: a spread (`updateMany({ ...scope, data })`) and the object shorthand (`updateMany({ where, data })`) both fire at `critical` on a scoped write — while `where: buildWhere(orgId)` does NOT, because that spelling puts the token back. The whole-argument form (`updateMany(args)`) used to fire here as well and no longer does: the trigger now requires the call line itself to OPEN the argument object (`updateMany({`) or to take no arguments at all (`updateMany()`), so a call handed its arguments by name — or one whose arguments open on the following line — is left alone instead of being judged on a `where:` token it never had the chance to spell. It under-reports in the mirror case: ANY `where:` in the body satisfies the veto, including a parameter type annotation, so `function f(where: object) { prisma.user.updateMany({ data }) }` is a genuine whole-table write this rule stays silent on. Both are the same defect seen from two sides, and the second is the one worth knowing about, since a silence here reads as a clean bill. Until the veto is scoped to the call rather than the body, treat a finding as `a where: token is absent from this function`, which is what it measures, rather than as the whole-table verdict its first sentence states.

`skip`/`take` pagination used with no `orderBy` in the enclosing function — without a stable sort, page boundaries can shift between requests (rows skipped or duplicated across pages). IF NO STABLE SORT IS ALREADY APPLIED: add an `orderBy:` on a column that is `@id`/`@unique` or the LEADING column of an `@@index` — merely stable is not enough, because sorting on a stable column no index leads (`createdAt` is the usual pick) trades the shifting page for a full table scan, which is what the sibling `orderby-unindexed` reports on the very line this remedy writes; if the column you want leads no index, add `@@index([column])` in the same change, and where it is not unique append `{ id: 'asc' }` as a tiebreaker so rows sharing a value cannot still swap places between pages — the index requirement is about the FIRST key of that list, and `orderby-unindexed` judges only the single-key object form, so its silence on an array is a decidable-subset boundary rather than a second opinion. The predicate is honest and the consequence is not, so read them apart: what is measured is that no `orderBy` TOKEN appears in this function, which is not the same as no stable sort being applied. Measured counterexample — `const opts = buildStableOrder(); findMany({ ...opts, skip, take })` fires, and the sort is right there in the spread, one call away. The veto is lexical and function-local, so an ordering built by a helper, passed in as a parameter, or spread from a variable is invisible to it and the finding still says the pages can shift.

`new PrismaClient()` constructed inside a function that looks like a request handler (a `req.`/`request.` member access, or a response-API call like `res.status(...)`/`res.send(...)` — deliberately NOT `res.json(`/`res.text(`, which a fetch `Response` also has, so a handler whose only response evidence is a bare `res.json(x)` is accepted as a miss rather than risking fetch-response false positives) — a fresh client per request exhausts the database connection pool under load. Hoist a single client to a module-level singleton instead.

A network call (`fetch`/`axios`/`got`) appears in the same function as a `$transaction(` — holding a database transaction open across a network round-trip extends lock hold time, and stalls with it if the external call stalls. IF THE NETWORK CALL REALLY HAPPENS WHILE THE TRANSACTION IS OPEN: move the network call outside the `$transaction` block. This is a CO-OCCURRENCE heuristic, not containment: the two halves are matched independently within one function body and nothing establishes that the network call happens WHILE the transaction is open. Measured counterexample — `await db.$transaction([...])` on one line and an unrelated `fetch(...)` on the next fires exactly like the dangerous shape, and there the transaction has already COMMITTED before the call is made, so no lock is held across anything. The claim above is what a real hit means; whether this hit is one is the reader's call. That is why it is `warning` and not `critical`, the standing every sibling in this pack takes for the same reason.

A database write (`create`/`update`/`delete`/`upsert`) on a DB-client-shaped receiver (`prisma`/`db`/`tx`/`client`/`repo`) whose promise is neither awaited, returned, nor chained — a failed write looks identical to a successful one. IF THE CALL IS NOT AN ELEMENT OF AN ARRAY TRANSACTION: await the call (or return it, or attach `.then()`/`.catch()`) — inside an array transaction that remedy breaks the code: `await prisma.$transaction([ a.create(...), b.create(...) ])` takes UN-awaited query builders as its elements, so awaiting one inside the array runs it immediately and OUTSIDE the transaction. That shape is vetoed structurally rather than by the reported line: the still-open opener lines above the call are read (up to 40 lines up), and an `await`/`return`/`yield`-ed `$transaction([`/`Promise.all([`/`Promise.allSettled([` among them waives the finding. The opener's own `await` is required, not decoration — an UNawaited `$transaction([...])` leaves the writes genuinely unawaited, so vetoing on the callee alone would hide a real bug; the cost is that `const p = prisma.$transaction([...]); await p;` still fires, which is the safe direction. Three more residuals, all of which likewise keep the site firing: a builder collected by `arr.push(prisma.x.update(...))` and spread in later (`$transaction([...ops])`) has `push(` as its enclosing call and is out of reach of any enclosing-call veto; an opener further up than the walk's cap is out of reach; and a multi-line template literal, a mid-line comment, or an unbalanced bracket crossed on the way up makes the walk decline rather than guess. The CALLBACK form is not vetoed and should not be — inside `$transaction(async (tx) => { ... })` an un-awaited write really is fire-and-forget and awaiting it really is the fix. Line-based otherwise, with a one-line lookback: an `await`/`return`/`.then`/`.catch`/`=>`/assignment on the call's own line counts as handled, as does a `=>` or `=` ending the line directly above (a formatter-wrapped arrow body or assignment); a continuation starting more than one line above the call is beyond that window and may still be flagged.

A `take`/`limit` pagination size is read directly from user input with no upper-bound clamp — a client can force the server to load and serialize an unbounded number of rows (memory/CPU exhaustion). Clamp it against a maximum (e.g. `Math.min(MAX_PAGE_SIZE, Number(req.query.limit))`).

A `.create(` call appears LEXICALLY AFTER a `findFirst`/`findOne`/`findUnique` read in the same function, with NEITHER a collision-atomic write (`connectOrCreate`, `.upsert(`, `ON CONFLICT`, `ON DUPLICATE KEY`) NOR a HANDLED unique violation anywhere in it — the reported line is the first create that actually follows a read, and "same function" means the NEAREST enclosing function, so a read in a sibling closure does not pair. A trigger line that sits inside NO parser-projected function span (a class-property initializer, a top-level statement) is read as ungated, and the pairing there widens back to the whole scanned symbol span. This is a TEXTUAL ORDER claim, not a dataflow one: it does not prove the create writes the row the read looked for, nor that both run on the same control-flow path. SAME-LINE NESTING RESIDUAL (a disclosed false negative shared by every rule that uses this order gate): on a single line "after" is decided by MATCH START OFFSET, so a read nested INSIDE the `.create(` call's own argument list reads as coming AFTER it and does not pair — an inline `prisma.member.create({ data: { orgId: (await prisma.org.findFirst({ where })).id } })` is silently NOT reported; only the multi-line spelling, or a same-line one whose read starts first, fires. When it is the check-then-act shape it names, two concurrent requests can both pass the check and both create a duplicate row. WHAT COUNTS AS A HANDLED VIOLATION, read narrowly and deliberately so: a COMPARISON against the vendor's collision code, not a mention of it — `err.code === "P2002"`, `e.cause.code === "P2002"`, `case "23505":`, `error.code == ER_DUP_ENTRY`, the reversed spelling of any of those, or an `instanceof` against a `UniqueConstraintError` class. A BARE TOKEN DOES NOT SILENCE THIS RULE: a log line reading `logger.info("...can raise 23505 downstream")`, a docs URL ending `#P2002`, or an error catalogue shipped in a response body all leave the finding standing. Until 2026-08-23 this arm matched the bare token anywhere in the function, and either of those two lines erased an unfixed check-then-act race — reproduced on a three-file probe before the narrowing. The narrowing costs recall in the other direction, disclosed rather than implied: a membership test (`["P2002", "P2003"].includes(e.code)`), a comparison against a NAMED constant (`e.code === DUPLICATE_KEY`), a substring test on the message (`err.message.includes("E11000")`) and MongoDB's numeric `err.code === 11000` are all real handlers this arm does not see, so the finding survives on them and has to be dismissed by hand. What it does match is TEXT over the whole function span — comment lines excluded, string literals NOT — so it is EVIDENCE the collision is handled, never proof: nothing ties the comparison to this create, and a comparison spelled inside a string literal counts all the same. FIRST RULE OUT A COLUMN PAIR THAT IS NOT MEANT TO BE UNIQUE — the remedy below opens by making the read's columns unique, and whether they are unique is a fact about YOUR domain that this finding neither establishes nor can see. Plenty of get-or-create shapes read a pair that legitimately repeats: one owner holding two linked accounts at the same external provider, two installs of one integration under a tenant, two records of a kind the product deliberately lets you hold more than one of. Where that is so the constraint is not a fix but two outages — the migration FAILS OUTRIGHT against any table that already holds a duplicate of the pair, and forced through, the second legitimate row is rejected at runtime and the feature that creates it stops working. So query the live table for duplicates of that pair, and check whether creating a second one is a supported action, BEFORE writing the migration. When the pair genuinely is not unique the answer is a DIFFERENT key, or none at all: add the column that actually distinguishes the two rows (the provider-side account id, the install id) so the constraint keys on the real identity — and where nothing distinguishes them this is not a duplicate-key problem, so serialize the check and the write instead, with a `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` row lock on the record that owns them or with serializable isolation. Where the pair IS unique: THE REMEDY IS THE UNIQUE CONSTRAINT, and then one of TWO ways of living with it — they are not interchangeable, and picking the wrong one is how a duplicate-row bug becomes an account takeover. (1) KEEP THE INSERT and handle the unique violation the constraint now raises (Prisma `P2002`, Postgres `23505`, MySQL `ER_DUP_ENTRY`), returning the same conflict the pre-check returned; this one is correct whatever the row holds, and seeing that handler is what makes this rule go quiet. (2) REPLACE THE INSERT with `upsert`/`connectOrCreate` — correct ONLY when OVERWRITING the existing row is what you want, because that is precisely what it does: an `upsert` keyed on `email` does not reject the second signup, it writes the caller's `update:` payload onto the account that already owns that address. On a row carrying a password hash, a session token, an identity provider or a role, taking (2) blindly hands the second caller the first caller's account, and the edit is often ONE TOKEN wide onto a repository helper that already wraps that `upsert` a few lines away — note that such a helper does NOT match the veto above, which reads `.upsert(` and not a name. So read what `update:` would overwrite before making that swap, and where the answer is a credential take (1). Wrapping the read+write in a `$transaction` alone does NOT close this race at the database's default READ COMMITTED isolation level — two concurrent transactions can both read empty and both insert.

A money-named identifier (`price`/`amount`/`balance`/`fee`/`cost`) compared with `==`/`===`/`!=`/`!==` against a float literal (e.g. `price === 19.99`) — floating-point rounding error makes strict equality on monetary values unreliable. Represent money as integer minor units (cents) or a decimal library.

A database write — an ORM call (`create`/`update`/`delete`/`upsert`/`updateMany`/`deleteMany`) or a RAW-SQL statement head (`INSERT INTO`, `UPDATE <table> SET`, `DELETE FROM`) opening a string literal or a line, matched UPPERCASE-only so English prose is not mistaken for SQL — appears in the same function as an empty `catch {}` block — the write's failure is caught and silently discarded, indistinguishable from success. IF THAT `catch {}` IS ACTUALLY AROUND THIS WRITE: log or rethrow the error instead of swallowing it. This is a CO-OCCURRENCE heuristic, not a link: the write and the empty `catch` are matched independently inside one function body, and nothing establishes that the catch WRAPS the write. Measured counterexample — a `try { JSON.parse(raw) } catch {}` guarding a parse, followed by an unrelated `create(...)` on a later line, fires identically, and there the write's failure is not swallowed at all: it propagates normally. Read a finding as "these two shapes share a function", then check whether the catch is actually around the write. `warning` and not `critical` for that gap.

Two independent write calls from different verb families — `create`/`createMany`/`insert` and `update`/`updateMany`/`delete`/`deleteMany`/`upsert` — appear in the same function with no transaction wrapping either. Each family also has a RAW-SQL arm: an `INSERT INTO` statement head counts as a create-family write, and an `UPDATE <table> SET`/`DELETE FROM` head as a mutate-family one, so an ORM-free backend (`db.prepare("INSERT INTO ...")`) is no longer silently exempt. Raw-SQL heads are matched UPPERCASE-only and must open a string literal or a line — the gate that separates SQL from English prose (`"Insert into the notes field"`), at the cost of not seeing lowercase SQL. This is a co-occurrence heuristic, not proof the two writes depend on each other, but when they do: a failure between the two calls leaves partial state, since the first write already committed and nothing rolls it back if the second throws. THE REMEDY IS CONDITIONAL. IF NOTHING BETWEEN THE TWO WRITES LEAVES THE DATABASE (no HTTP or SDK call, no mail, no payment charge, no queue publish), wrap both writes in `$transaction(...)` (or a bare `transaction(...)` call, or an explicit `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` transaction, or a driver batch such as D1's `batch([...])`, all four of which are recognized and veto this finding), or replace the pair with a single write. IF AN EXTERNAL CALL SITS BETWEEN THEM, DO NOT WRAP THE PAIR: an interactive transaction then holds a pooled connection and the first write's row locks across that round trip, and one slow response trips the ORM's own ceiling on it (Prisma's interactive default aborts at 5s), rolling the block back so NOTHING is stored — including the row that commits today, under a handler that logs the abort and still renders success. Split the boundary instead: a transaction on each side of the external call, or the call moved out of the block, plus a retry or reconciliation path for the second write. Suppress a vetted case (e.g. two genuinely independent writes) with `// zzop-multi-write-no-tx-ok`.

An update that recomputes a field as `<ident> + 1`/`<ident> - 1` appears LEXICALLY AFTER a read (`findUnique`/`findFirst`/`findOne`/`findById`) in the same function — the reported line is the first such arithmetic entry that actually follows a read, and "same function" means the NEAREST enclosing function, so a read in a sibling closure does not pair. A trigger line that sits inside NO parser-projected function span (a class-property initializer, a top-level statement) is read as ungated, and the pairing there widens back to the whole scanned symbol span. This is a TEXTUAL ORDER claim, not a dataflow one: it does not prove the arithmetic recomputes the field the read returned. Any `field: value + 1`-shaped object entry that follows the read trips it, even one unrelated to it (e.g. a `take: cursor + 1` pagination bound). When it is the shape it names, read-then-arithmetic-update is not atomic, and two concurrent requests can both read the same starting value and both write the same incremented result, silently losing one of the two increments. Use the ORM's atomic increment/decrement (e.g. Prisma's `{ increment: 1 }`/`{ decrement: 1 }`), a DB-side `$inc`, or a `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` row lock instead of read-then-write arithmetic.

A connection acquired via `pool.connect(`/`getConnection(`/`acquireConnection(` is never released (`.release(`/`.destroy(`/`.end(`) or returned (`return conn`/`connection`/`client`) anywhere in this function — under load, each unreleased connection stays checked out of the pool, and once the pool is exhausted every later request stalls waiting for one to free up. IF NO HELPER CALLED FROM HERE ALREADY RELEASES IT: release it in a `finally` block, use a `using`/`await using` declaration (recognized, does not fire), or use the pool's single-shot query shortcut instead of a manual acquire/release pair. Note the limitation: this only sees the current function's own body — a release happening inside a helper function called from here is invisible to this check and still fires; verify before refactoring, or suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-connection-no-release-ok`.

A DB/connection client or pool (`new PrismaClient()`/`new Pool()`/`new Sequelize()`/`new MongoClient()`/`new IORedis()`/`new Redis()`, or a `createPool`/`createClient`/`createConnection` call) is constructed structurally inside a loop body — verified against the parser's projected loop spans (the constructor call's own line falls within a loop statement's or array-iteration callback's span), not merely co-occurring with loop syntax somewhere in the same function. To avoid firing on same-named non-database constructs (a worker-pool `new Pool()`, an API `createClient()`, a raw-socket `createConnection()`), the rule only scans files that import a database driver/ORM. Allocating a fresh connection/pool per iteration exhausts the database connection pool under any real iteration count. Hoist the client to a module-level singleton, or construct it once outside the loop and reuse it across iterations. This sharpens `client-new-in-handler` (which fires on request-handler co-occurrence — a `new PrismaClient()` alongside `req.`/`res.` evidence anywhere in the function — rather than on loop containment); a handler that constructs a client inside a loop can trip both rules on the same line, which is expected since they assert different things.

A database write — either an ORM call (`create`/`createMany`/`update`/`updateMany`/`delete`/`deleteMany`/`upsert`/`insert`/`save`) on a DB-client-shaped receiver (`prisma`/`db`/`tx`/`client`/`repo`/...), or a RAW-SQL statement head (`INSERT INTO`, `UPDATE <table> SET`, `DELETE FROM`) opening a string literal or a line — executes structurally inside a loop body, verified against the parser's projected loop spans, not mere co-occurrence, while the enclosing function opens no transaction (no `$transaction(`, bare `transaction(` call, SQL `BEGIN`, or driver `batch(`). Raw-SQL heads are matched UPPERCASE-only, the gate that separates SQL from English prose, at the cost of not seeing lowercase SQL. Each iteration autocommits independently: a mid-loop failure leaves the already-committed prefix behind with nothing to roll it back, and a caller retry double-applies the rows that already committed. This is the loop-containment-proven sibling of `multi-write-no-tx`, which requires two different write-verb families (a create-family call and a mutate-family call) to co-occur in the same function — it structurally misses a single-verb write repeated once per loop iteration, exactly the shape this rule catches. THE REMEDY IS CONDITIONAL, AND THE WRONG BRANCH RE-SENDS WORK THAT ALREADY LEFT THE PROCESS. IF THE LOOP BODY TOUCHES NOTHING OUTSIDE THE DATABASE (no mail or SMS, no payment or webhook call, no queue publish), wrap the loop body in `$transaction(...)`, or replace the per-row writes with a batch `createMany`/`updateMany` call; `$transaction(` is one of this rule's own veto tokens, so that edit also turns this finding off. IF THE LOOP BODY DOES ANY OF THOSE THINGS, DO NOT WRAP IT — suppress this finding with the marker named at the end instead. The per-iteration autocommit is then the correct at-least-once ordering, not an oversight: do the irreversible thing, then record that it was done. A transaction inverts that, because the rollback deletes the record while the side effect itself is already gone — a cron that sends a reminder on one line and records it on the next re-sends its entire backlog on the following run. BEFORE PRESCRIBING REPLAY-SAFETY TO YOURSELF, CHECK WHETHER THE LOOP ALREADY HAS IT: a query above the loop that reads what was already recorded and filters the iteration against it is the same defence, and this rule cannot see it. Where it is genuinely absent, adding it may be a schema migration rather than a local edit — the recorded table often carries no unique key to `upsert` on.

A `.create(`/`.insert(` call whose own line is verified to sit inside a loop body (via the parser's projected loop spans) appears LEXICALLY AFTER a `findFirst`/`findUnique`/`findOne`/`exists` read in the NEAREST enclosing function, and neither a `connectOrCreate`/`upsert`/`ON CONFLICT`/`ON DUPLICATE KEY` guard nor a HANDLED unique violation appears anywhere in that function — "handled" carrying the same narrow reading `find-then-create-no-unique`'s message spells out (a COMPARISON against the vendor collision code — `err.code === "P2002"`, `case "23505":`, `instanceof UniqueConstraintError` — never a bare mention of the token), because the two rules name ONE race and a function that has closed it must go quiet under BOTH: this rule carried no such arm until 2026-08-23, so a handled collision went silent under the sibling and still fired here, delegating its remedy to a message that was absent from that run's output. A trigger line that sits inside NO parser-projected function span (a class-property initializer, a top-level statement) is read as ungated, and the pairing there widens back to the whole scanned symbol span. The create is loop-proven and order-proven relative to the read; the read is NOT itself proven to sit in the loop, and the order is textual, not dataflow (nothing proves the create writes the row the read looked for). SAME-LINE NESTING RESIDUAL (a disclosed false negative shared by every rule that uses this order gate): on a single line "after" is decided by MATCH START OFFSET, so a read nested INSIDE the `.create(`/`.insert(` call's own argument list reads as coming AFTER it and does not pair — an inline `prisma.member.create({ data: { orgId: (await prisma.org.findFirst({ where })).id } })` inside the loop is silently NOT reported; only the multi-line spelling, or a same-line one whose read starts first, fires. This is the batch get-or-create shape: two concurrent workers (or an overlapping retry) can both observe "absent" for the same key on an iteration and both insert a duplicate row. It sharpens `find-then-create-no-unique` (a whole-function co-occurrence heuristic) by additionally loop-proving the create, and can fire alongside it on the overlapping shape. FIRST RULE OUT A COLUMN PAIR THAT IS NOT MEANT TO BE UNIQUE — a pair one owner may legitimately hold twice (two linked accounts at the same external provider, two installs of one integration) takes no such constraint: the migration FAILS OUTRIGHT against a table that already holds a duplicate of it, and forced through, the second legitimate row is rejected and the feature that creates it stops working. Where the pair IS unique, add a unique constraint; that precondition, the two ways of meeting it, and the overwrite caution that decides between them are spelled out in `find-then-create-no-unique`'s message and apply here verbatim. A `$transaction` wrap alone does not close this race at the database's default READ COMMITTED isolation level.

An idempotency key is assigned a FRESH random value (`randomUUID()`/`uuidv4()`/`nanoid()`/`cuid()`/...) on a line that sits structurally inside a loop/retry body — verified against the parser's projected loop spans (the assignment's own line falls within a loop statement's or array-iteration callback's span), not merely co-occurring with loop syntax somewhere in the same function — so every attempt carries a DIFFERENT key and the server treats each retry as a brand-new request, defeating the idempotency the key exists to provide. The key is present and correctly named, so this survives ordinary code review. Generate the key ONCE before the loop and reuse it across every attempt, or derive it deterministically from the request payload (e.g. a hash of a stable business id) instead of a random generator.

A `$transaction(`/`.transaction(` call on a DB-client-shaped receiver (`prisma`/`db`/`client`) whose promise is neither awaited, returned, nor chained — it runs detached, and the handler can send its response before the transaction commits or fails. Await the call (or return it, or attach `.then()`/`.catch()`).

A `BEGIN`/`beginTransaction()`/`startTransaction()` call and a `COMMIT`/`.commit()` call both appear somewhere in the same function — this is a co-occurrence heuristic, not proof COMMIT actually follows BEGIN or that nothing is nested between them, but when it's a genuine manual transaction: no `ROLLBACK`/`.rollback()` appears anywhere in the function either, so an error raised between BEGIN and COMMIT has nothing to release it, and the half-open transaction poisons the pooled connection for whichever request borrows it next. Wrap the work in a try/catch that issues `ROLLBACK` (or `.rollback()`) on error, or use the ORM's managed `$transaction(...)` wrapper instead of manual BEGIN/COMMIT.

An empty `catch {}` appears in the same function as a `$transaction(`/`@Transactional`/`beginTransaction()` call — swallowing the error prevents the throw that would trigger a rollback, so a partially-failed transaction can commit as if it succeeded. This is a co-occurrence heuristic: it doesn't prove the empty catch wraps the transaction's body, only that both patterns appear in the same function span. Log the error and rethrow it (or handle rollback explicitly) instead of swallowing it.

A `$transaction(`/`@Transactional` span also matches a money/inventory-named identifier (`balance`/`amount`/`payment`/`wallet`/`ledger`/`charge`/`refund`/`invoice`/`inventory`/`stock`) and a write call (`update`/`create`/`upsert`/`increment`/`decrement`), but sets no explicit isolation level (`isolationLevel`/`Serializable`/`RepeatableRead`) and takes no `FOR UPDATE` row lock — this is a co-occurrence heuristic, not proof the write actually touches the money field or that it runs inside the transaction body, and whether the database's default isolation is actually unsafe here depends on the target engine (e.g. READ COMMITTED on Postgres permits lost updates and write skew for a read-modify-write; other engines and defaults differ). Treat this as a review nudge, not a confirmed defect. RAISING THE LEVEL IS NOT FREE, AND THE COST LANDS ON THIS EXACT PATH: `Serializable`/`RepeatableRead` do not make the second writer wait, they ABORT one of the two with serialization failure `40001`, which Prisma surfaces as `P2034` and does NOT retry — so a payment handler that was quietly racing starts throwing under concurrency instead, and a webhook sender that sees the 500 re-delivers against a transaction that may already have committed. Set an explicit isolation level TOGETHER WITH a bounded retry around the whole `$transaction` (catch `P2034`, re-run the callback, cap the attempts, and keep the callback idempotent because it will be re-run) — e.g. `{ isolationLevel: Prisma.TransactionIsolationLevel.Serializable }` — or take a `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` row lock for the money-critical read-modify-write instead, which makes the second writer WAIT rather than abort and so needs no retry path at all.

A call on the transaction-scoped client (`tx.<model>.<method>(...)`, or a bare `prisma`/`db`/`client`/`repo`-receiver call) executes structurally inside a loop body — verified against the parser's projected loop spans (the call's own line falls within a loop statement's or array-iteration callback's span), not merely co-occurring with loop syntax somewhere in the same function — while the enclosing function also opens a `$transaction(...)` block. This is a co-occurrence heuristic for the tx-wrapping, same discipline as `external-call-and-tx`: it confirms `$transaction(` appears somewhere in the same function, not that this specific loop sits inside that transaction's own callback body — but when it does, the transaction stays open, and its underlying database locks held, for the entire loop's duration, so lock hold time scales with the number of rows processed inside it: every other transaction contending for the same rows/table queues up for as long as the loop takes to run, and one slow iteration (a large row, a stalled dependency) prolongs the hold for every row already processed. This is the mirror image of `write-in-loop-no-tx` (which fires on the SAME loop-containment shape only when NO enclosing transaction exists) — the two are mutually exclusive on a given line by construction, so they never co-fire. Move per-row reads out of the transaction where the data doesn't need to be read inside it, or replace the per-row calls with a single batch `updateMany`/`createMany`/`findMany` call inside the transaction so the lock is held for one round trip instead of N. Suppress a vetted case (e.g. a bounded, small row count) with `// zzop-tx-and-db-call-in-loop-ok`.
